source: Sarukkai, Xie, Fatahalian (2025) Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks main results
finding: Closest multi-seed test of learned case value for a frozen LLM. Agent keeps its own successful trajectories as in-context examples (top-k by similarity). Naive accumulation already gives large gains. Adding a learned per-trajectory value (exemplar curation) adds a smaller extra gain, and it varies by task.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini, 5 seeds. Fixed small human DB: ALFWorld 0.73, InterCode-SQL 0.75, Wordcraft 0.55. Naive accumulation (Traj-Bootstrap): 0.89, 0.79, 0.64. Plus exemplar-level curation (learned Q): 0.90, 0.81, 0.72. Extra gain of learned value over naive accumulation: +1, +2, +8 points. Plus DB-level and exemplar: 0.93, 0.82, 0.69. Top-k similarity retrieval, k=6 (ALFWorld, SQL), 10 (Wordcraft).
limits: Weaker backbone (gpt-4o-mini), not a frontier model. The comparison is curated database vs uncurated database under the same similarity retrieval, not learned value vs similarity at retrieval time. Spreads of 0.01 to 0.03 mean the +1 on ALFWorld is not clearly outside noise. Text and table disagree on two Wordcraft numbers (0.71/0.67 in text vs 0.72/0.69 in table).
agent_relevance: Best evidence found for gaps 1 and 7: learned value on top of already-relevant similarity retrieval is worth 1 to 8 points, small where the base already works (ALFWorld).

source: Sarukkai, Xie, Fatahalian (2025) Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks exemplar value metric
finding: The learned value is simple: Q(trajectory) = retrieval-frequency-weighted success rate of tasks where it was retrieved. Only trajectories retrieved for at least 3 tasks get a value. Per task, only the highest-Q successful trajectory is kept. Some successful trajectories lead to later failures when reused, because they succeeded in spite of bad steps.
numbers: Equation 1 in paper. Figure 4: databases built from the top-1 Q trajectory per task beat databases built from the bottom-1 Q successful trajectory on ALFWorld and Wordcraft (exact values only in the figure). Min 3 distinct retrieved tasks per Q estimate.
quote: some trajectories marked as successful lead to failures when retrieved
limits: No exploration bonus: Q is a plain empirical mean after a fixed training phase, so this is greedy value, not UCB or Thompson. Bank is frozen at test time.
agent_relevance: A cheap value rule (empirical success rate when retrieved, min 3 uses) is enough to rank successful cases; we do not need a bandit to start.

source: Sarukkai, Xie, Fatahalian (2025) Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks cost and pass@k comparison
finding: Compares the curation approach against spending effort on repeated attempts. Curated databases give single-attempt success equal to 2 to 5 attempts from the fixed database. Cost: curation needs N times more training inference (N parallel databases); test cost is unchanged.
numbers: Fixed-DB pass@1..5: ALFWorld 0.73/0.87/0.92/0.94/0.96; SQL 0.75/0.78/0.80/0.81/0.82; Wordcraft 0.55/0.62/0.64/0.66/0.72. Traj-Bootstrap single attempt (0.89, 0.79, 0.64) lies between pass@2 and pass@3. DB+Exemplar curation (0.93, 0.82, 0.69) lies between pass@3 and pass@5. ALFWorld: +20 points from accumulation vs +15 from upgrading gpt-4o-mini to gpt-4o.
limits: Costs given as call counts (N times training calls), not tokens. Pass@k assumes a perfect oracle verifier, so best-of-N is flattered. Training tasks are separate from test tasks.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 8: a one-off value-building phase can pay back against best-of-N at test time, but only if the same task family recurs and a success label exists in training.

source: Sarukkai, Xie, Fatahalian (2025) Self-Generated In-Context Examples Improve LLM Agents for Sequential Decision-Making Tasks train/test separation and variance
finding: Training and test tasks are distinct, so gains are transfer, not repeats. But the outcome of naive accumulation varies between runs because early lucky or unlucky examples snowball. This is the stated reason for database-level curation.
numbers: Figure 1: five trials on InterCode-SQL end at visibly different success rates after identical procedures (roughly 0.72 to 0.78 by eye). Appendix F.2 separates single-task optimisation, mixed train-test evaluation (which it criticises) and train-then-test on distinct scenarios (its setting). Five seeds in every table.
limits: Seed spread is read from a figure, not a table. Backbones gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4o only.
agent_relevance: Seed variance of an accumulated bank is as large as some claimed value gains. Any test of a learned case value needs many seeds and fresh test tasks.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory runtime vs frozen-bank transfer
finding: MemRL reports two settings. Runtime learning (same items seen again across 10 epochs) shows a large gain over plain RAG. Transfer (bank frozen, held-out tasks) shows a much smaller gain. Recomputing both on the same four benchmarks shows about two thirds of the runtime advantage over RAG disappears on held-out tasks.
numbers: My computation from Tables 1 and 2. Four shared benchmarks (BigCodeBench, OS, DB, ALFWorld). Runtime last-epoch success: MemRL mean 0.823 vs RAG 0.7415, gap 8.15 points. Frozen-bank transfer: MemRL 0.794 vs RAG 0.7655, gap 2.8 points; vs MemP 0.766; vs no memory 0.709 (gap 8.5). So held-out advantage over RAG is about 35% of the runtime advantage.
limits: Different task splits per setting, so 8.15 vs 2.8 is indicative, not a clean paired test. Transfer table uses 'best validation results', so selection may inflate it. No seeds or error bars. Last-epoch success still reuses training items.
agent_relevance: Closes part of gap 4: roughly 65% of the runtime gain over similarity-only RAG looks like repeat exposure, not transfer. A learned value still helps on held-out tasks by about 3 points.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) MemRL: Self-Evolving Agents via Runtime Reinforcement Learning on Episodic Memory task structure, similarity and HLE memorisation
finding: Appendix B admits the HLE gain is runtime memorisation of repeated hard items, not pattern transfer. Gains are larger on multi-step tasks than single-step, and track within-dataset task similarity.
numbers: Table 4 cumulative-success gain over MemP: ALFWorld +6.2 pp (91.9 to 98.1), OS +6.2 (74.2 to 80.4), HLE +3.6 (57.0 to 60.6), BigCodeBench +2.5 (60.2 to 62.7). Single-task reflection vs cross-task: MemRL gain +9.0 on OS, tie on HLE (0.606 vs 0.610).
quote: the gain in HLE stems from Runtime Memorization
limits: Cumulative success counts any-epoch success, which flatters repeats. No seeds. Self-reported.
agent_relevance: Supports gaps 3 and 4: learned value pays on recurring multi-step families; on scattered one-shot questions it mostly memorises.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior memory addition and evaluator noise
finding: Four agents, streams of thousands of tasks, frozen LLM. Adding every run to memory hurts. Adding only runs passed by an evaluator helps only if the evaluator is good. A weak automatic evaluator can be worse than keeping the fixed starting memory. Best direct evidence for gap 5 (label noise).
numbers: Table 1 (RegAgent SR / EHRAgent ACC / AgentDriver SR / CIC-IoT ACC): fixed memory 67.53 / 16.75 / 40.11 / 71.50. Add-all 55.48 / 13.05 / 32.32 / 59.90. Coarse LLM judge C1 63.18 / 26.19 / 36.92 / 74.00. C2 65.78 / 32.21 / 40.01 / 68.80. C3 (judge fine-tuned on 300 trajectories) 67.35 / 34.66 / 47.37 / 79.50. Strict human-grade evaluator 70.95 / 38.50 / 51.00 / 85.40. Memory grows to about 900 to 4100 records.
limits: Memory retrieved by input similarity top-k; learned utility is used only for add and delete, not selection. Single run per cell, no error bars. The synthetic RegAgent task rewards copying.
agent_relevance: Rule of thumb: an untuned LLM judge can leave the bank worse than a small fixed bank; a judge tuned on a few hundred labelled runs recovers most of the gain.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior history-based deletion by learned utility
finding: Deleting records whose average downstream utility (success of tasks that retrieved them, at least n retrievals) is low improves results when the evaluator is strict, but is unstable with a coarse LLM evaluator. Deleted records had lower correctness than retained ones.
numbers: Table 2, strict evaluator, history deletion vs no deletion: RegAgent 69.80 vs 70.95; EHRAgent 42.06 vs 38.67; AgentDriver 51.81 vs 51.00; CIC-IoT 89.60 vs 85.40. Coarse C1: EHRAgent 33.55 vs 25.91 (up), AgentDriver 34.00 vs 36.92 (down), CIC-IoT 73.70 vs 74.00. Table 4 (EHRAgent, coarse): retained correctness 44.1 / 49.1 / 54.8 vs deleted 36.3 / 32.1 / 48.2 for three judges. Periodic deletion cuts memory to roughly a quarter to a third with small loss.
limits: Single run, no intervals; 1 point differences are not distinguishable from noise. Table columns read from garbled text. Deletion, not selection.
agent_relevance: A utility-based retire rule is worth having only with a reliable success label; with a noisy label use periodic pruning instead.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior distribution shift, capacity limits, error propagation
finding: Under an abrupt task-distribution shift mid-stream, simple addition plus utility deletion keeps performance close to the no-shift run. A fixed memory cap (100 to 180 records) with utility-based eviction still beats the fixed memory. Wrong stored outputs are copied and spread (experience-following).
numbers: Figure 7: gap to the no-shift variant is small in general; in AgentDriver strict addition alone exceeded the no-shift run; on EHRAgent history deletion lagged combined deletion. Experience-following: Pearson r near 1 between input and output similarity for RegAgent. With strict addition AgentDriver approaches and after about 2000 executions surpasses the ground-truth-fed memory variant.
limits: Shift built by reordering existing test inputs, not a true new domain. No seeds.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 3: with a good evaluator and periodic deletion, utility-style memory survives one shift; no study varies how far tasks drift.

source: Kuleshov and Precup (2014) Algorithms for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: Large simulation study of bandit rules. Simple epsilon-greedy and softmax beat UCB1 in most settings. UCB1 converges slowest, and UCB degrades fastest as the number of arms grows.
numbers: Twelve instances (K = 2, 5, 10, 50 arms; three reward variances), 1000 steps, parameters tuned per instance. Softmax had lowest total regret on all tasks except high variance (sigma=1) with K<=10, where UCB1-Tuned was ahead. Boltzmann beat its closest competitor by 10% to 100%. Example regret at K=50: UCB1 296, UCB1-Tuned 119 to 120, softmax about 32, epsilon-greedy about 29 to 40.
limits: Parameters tuned per instance, which favours tunable heuristics. Stationary arms. Not LLM cases.
agent_relevance: For a case bank with many candidate arms and few pulls, greedy plus a small random rule is a fair default; a UCB bonus is not free.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem
finding: Proves logarithmic finite-time regret for UCB1, UCB2 and a decaying epsilon-greedy rule, and compares them on seven simulated reward sets. Tuned epsilon-greedy almost always did best; UCB1-Tuned was close but has no proof.
numbers: Section 4.1: tuned epsilon-n-greedy performs almost always best; exceptions where several bad arms differ a lot (distributions 12, 14). UCB1-Tuned comparable to a well-tuned greedy; UCB2 similar but slightly worse. Untuned epsilon-greedy degrades quickly.
quote: An optimally tuned n-GREEDY performs almost always best
limits: Simulations on stationary independent arms; tuning epsilon needs knowledge of the reward gap. Context-free.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'Auer unopened' part of gap 9: the classic source already shows the bonus is not what wins in practice.

source: Chapelle and Li (2011) An empirical evaluation of Thompson sampling
finding: Thompson sampling beats UCB and epsilon-greedy in simulation, display-ad CTR and news recommendation. A damped version (posterior reshaped, alpha<1) did slightly better. Exploit-only (pure greedy) was a strong baseline in the contextual ad setting.
numbers: Display advertising CTR regret % (Table 2): Thompson 4.45 / 3.72 / 3.81 (alpha 0.25/0.5/1); LinUCB 4.99 / 4.22 / 4.14; epsilon-greedy 5.05 / 4.98 / 5.22; exploit-only 5.00; random 31.95. Simulated Bernoulli bandits: best arm 0.5, others 0.5 minus gap, K = 10 or 100, 100 repeats, regret about logarithmic.
limits: Hourly batch updates, huge traffic, millions of pulls. Case banks see far fewer pulls per arm. Delayed feedback favours Thompson (randomised) over UCB (deterministic).
agent_relevance: If we want an exploration rule, Thompson on a Beta posterior per case is the cheapest tested alternative; best Thompson 3.72 vs exploit-only 5.00 is a gain of 1.3 regret points, and LinUCB (4.14) beat exploit-only by under 1.

source: Garivier and Moulines (2008) On upper-confidence bound policies for non-stationary bandit problems
finding: Classic UCB assumes fixed arm rewards and fails to track a changing best arm. For abrupt changes, no policy can beat a regret rate of about sqrt(T); discounted UCB and sliding-window UCB come within a log factor of that bound.
numbers: Lower bound order sqrt(T) (vs log T when stationary). With breakpoints growing as T^beta, D-UCB and SW-UCB regret is O(T^((1+beta)/2) log T); with few breakpoints O(sqrt(T log T)). Simulation with two reward swaps (t=3000 and 5000): discounted and sliding-window UCB track the new best arm.
limits: Theory for abrupt changes in independent arms; case value under drift also changes with the query, not only with time.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 3 in theory: if case value drifts, use a discount or window on the value estimate; plain running means (as in d02) lag. The price is a worse regret rate.

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank success-only vs both outcomes, and judge noise
finding: Lessons distilled from both successes and failures beat success-only for this method. Baselines that store raw successes do not gain from failures. Label noise barely matters: with the success label simulated down to random (50%), memory still beats no memory.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash. Success-only vs with failures: ReasoningBank 46.5 to 49.7; Synapse 40.6 to 41.7; AWM 44.4 to 42.2 (falls). Judge accuracy measured 72.7%. Simulated judge accuracy sweep (figure, read by eye): about 52 at 100%, about 49.7 at 70 to 80%, about 47.6 at 50 to 60%. No-memory baseline 39.0 (earlier evidence).
limits: Memory is LLM-distilled strategies, not cases picked by learned value, so label noise changes what is written, not what is retrieved. Figure values approximate. Single run.
agent_relevance: Weakens the gap-5 worry for distilled lessons (noise costs about 5 of 13 points), but d07 shows raw-record banks are far more sensitive. Failures help when turned into lessons, not stored raw.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory similarity retrieval baseline and task similarity
finding: Streaming benchmark, ten datasets, Gemini-2.5 Flash and Claude 3.7 Sonnet. A plain top-k similarity retrieval baseline (ExpRAG) is competitive with many more complex memory systems. Memory gain tracks how similar tasks are within a dataset.
numbers: Correlation of ReMem gain over history baseline with within-dataset task similarity: Pearson 0.717 (Gemini 2.5 Flash), 0.563 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet). Single-turn improvements called 'moderate'; ReMem 0.65 average exact match with Gemini. Clustered multi-turn sets (PDDL, ALFWorld) gain most; diverse sets (AIME-25, GPQA) gain least. Smaller models benefit most.
limits: No learned-value selector is tested. Tables are garbled in the PDF text, so per-cell numbers were not used. Single run, no error bars.
agent_relevance: Independent hint for gap 1: on frontier backbones, similarity retrieval captures most of the memory gain, and no learned-value baseline exists on this benchmark yet.

source: Wei et al. (2026) Evo-Memory: Benchmarking LLM agent test-time learning with self-evolving memory failed experiences and difficulty order
finding: When failed trajectories are stored without filtering, most memory baselines degrade; the method that actively refines memory stays robust. Easy-to-hard vs hard-to-easy order changes baseline results a lot.
numbers: Table 3 (ALFWorld success/progress, Claude 3.7 Sonnet): ExpRAG 0.76 / 0.90, ReMem 0.92 / 0.96, other baselines about 0.47 to 0.62 success. Gemini-2.5 Flash: ReMem 0.57 / 0.76 on ALFWorld. HardEasy up to 0.94 / 0.97 for ReMem.
limits: Partly garbled table. ReMem rewrites memory with the LLM; it is not a value learner. Single run.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 7: raw failures hurt unless gated; the open need is a learned value that marks failures as 'avoid' instead of deleting them.

source: Levy, Bogin, Berant (2023) Diverse demonstrations improve in-context compositional generalization
finding: Choosing demonstrations as a set that covers needed structures beats top-k by similarity, especially when no single demonstration is close. The advantage shrinks on i.i.d. splits. Coverage methods beat a plain diversity (DPP) method on 7 of 10 splits.
numbers: GeoQuery, Codex without fine-tuning, full test set, single seed (Table 3): Top-K 88.9 / 74.7 / 69.4 / 65.8 vs Cover-LS 91.4 / 81.6 / 76.3 / 70.0 (iid / template / TMCD / length). One failure: Cover-LS on SMCalFlow 0-C split, about 0 accuracy, because the structure predictor scored 0.
limits: Semantic parsing with Codex (old model). Structure coverage needs a predictor. No learned success value, so this does not test gap 10 directly.
agent_relevance: Set-level coverage is a cheap, value-free fix for gap 6 at K of 4 to 20; it is a different axis from learned value and has not been combined with it.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Repeated sampling raises coverage a lot, but choosing the right answer without a verifier plateaus near 100 samples. This is the competing use of tokens against building case values.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9% with one sample, 56% with 250 samples (coverage, unit tests as verifier); single-sample SOTA then 43%. MATH, Llama-3-8B: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%. CodeContests Gemma-2B: 0.02% to 7.1% at 10,000 samples.
limits: Tasks with automatic verifiers get the full benefit; without them selection is the bottleneck. No case memory involved.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: best-of-N beats value learning only when a cheap verifier exists. The same outcome label that lets a case value be learned also makes best-of-N work; the budget split is untested.

source: Aamodt and Plaza (1994) Case-based reasoning: foundational issues, methodological variations, and system approaches
finding: The founding CBR review treats retention as part of the cycle. The case base is updated whether the solve worked or failed. Failures may be stored as separate failure cases and give a 'reminding' of past failures. Retrieval indexes are tuned by outcome: features that led to successful cases get stronger links, features that led to bad retrievals get weaker (PATDEX relevance weights from success or failure feedback). New cases can be merged with near duplicates.
numbers: No experiments. Section 8 'Case Retainment - Learning': extract, index and integrate steps.
limits: Conceptual review of 1990s systems (CASEY, PROTOS, PATDEX, CHEF). No growth-rate or utility-problem numbers.
agent_relevance: Closes the 'Aamodt unopened' part of gap 9: outcome-based tuning of retrieval and storing failures were already standard CBR; LLM papers re-derive them. Retention options (merge near duplicates, keep failures as warnings) carry over to class records.

source: Gap note: items searched and not found (this pass)
finding: Web search quota was exhausted, so only direct paper pulls from arXiv, NIPS and university sites were used. No paper was found that (a) compares UCB vs Thompson vs greedy Q vs epsilon-greedy over a case bank with regret for an LLM, (b) ablates success-only vs both outcomes under a learned selector, (c) combines learned value with diversity-aware set selection, or (d) credits several co-shown cases. Thompson (1933) and the 1990s case-based reinforcement learning papers were not obtained.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Absence is relative to this search only; Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv search were rate limited.
agent_relevance: These stay open and are candidates for our own small experiments.
